newsitem.title: USA: Florida schools, districts may be too large--study.
newsitem.headline: Florida schools, districts may be too large--study.

text.p: Rather than spend more money on school operating costs, Florida should break up some of its massive school districts and reduce the number of pupils per school, a study by the James Madison Institute recommends.
"Florida needs to seriously consider whether it has too few school districts and schools that are too large," the report concluded.
The Tallahassee-based institute is a think tank devoted to "free-market ideas on public policy issues" and provided a draft copy of its study to Reuters.
The report said that despite the perception that Florida spends little on education, it actually funds its schools fairly well.
Florida spent $5,305 per pupil in fiscal 1994, more than California or Texas and more than any other Southeastern state except Virgnia, the study said.
The state also spends more on education than any other program, but its educational performance lags, the study said.

Florida's high school graduation rate is 67.8 percent, compared to a national average of 76.5 percent. Florida also ranks low in other measures of ecudational achievement, including average SAT scores and college degrees conferred.
But the study said, "Rather than simply spend more money on education, Florida should experiment with structural changes in its schools and colleges."
High on the list of recommended changes is breaking up the state's large school districts into smaller, more manageable districts.

Florida school districts are countywide, so it has only 67 districts, substantially fewer than other states of similiar size and population. The largest is in Dade County, which encompasses the Miami area and has about 334,000 students.

Florida also has fewer schools per population than most states. The average school size in Florida is 780 students, more than 50 percent larger than the national average. Florida has not built enough schools to keep up with rapid increases in its school-age population, resulting in classroom crowding that contributes to the perception that education is underfunded.
A bill allowing the large districts to split failed during the most recent legislative session. Lawmakers also failed to reach agreement on a statewide funding program for school construction.

The institute's report comes as Florida teachers and other groups are collecting petition signatures to force a referendum on a constitutional amendment requiring that at least 40 percent of general fund revenues be spent on education.
Schools currently get about 35 percent of those revenues. The proposal would increase their budgets by about $2 billion.

The Madison Institute study also recommended other changes, including allowing parents to choose which schools their children attend, and measuring performance by outcomes such as test scores and graduation rates, rather than by traditional measures such as per-pupil spending and the number and variety of courses taught.
